comment: Step 6 - React 19.
This is the version the whole migration line is named for, and this is the
step it arrives at.  The line's plan gives this step five React 19 constructs:
use(), Actions with useActionState/useFormStatus, ref as prop, <Context> as
provider, and propTypes/defaultProps removed.  Measured on the tree this step
starts from, four of the five have no subject at all: zero createContext, zero
forwardRef and zero callback refs, zero <form> and zero onSubmit, zero
defaultProps, and no promise or context anywhere for use() to read - the
sixty-four context reads in this tree are the router's useOutletContext, which
is not React context, and the data layer is RTK Query, which does not suspend.
Manufacturing a subject for each of them would be writing new features and
calling it a migration.  The fifth has a subject: three components carry a
propTypes object and the package that builds it is still a dependency.
So the step is the upgrade and its own consequences, which is what the survey
of this tree says a React 19 migration of it actually is:
- react and react-dom to 19;
- react-redux from 7.2.9, whose peer range stops at React 18, to a release
that declares React 19.  This is the forcing function.  npm ci - which
this step's spec requires, the same as the four before it - fails outright
on React 19 beside react-redux 7.2.9, so the tree does not install, does
not build, and scores nothing.  Measured: a probe of exactly that pairing
finished in seven seconds with 'dependency install failed' and every gate
unevaluated.  react-redux is also the only dependency of this tree whose
peer range excludes React 19: react-icons declares '*', react-router-dom
'>=16.8', and @reduxjs/toolkit already lists ^19.  One edge, and it is a
hard one.
- the propTypes layer gone: the three declarations, the three imports, and
the dependency.
and everything the five steps before it built, held.
What this step does NOT gate, and why:
- Anything about use(), Actions, ref-as-prop or <Context>.  There is no
subject; a gate would be asking a candidate to invent one.
- An absence of overrides or of legacy-peer-deps in the tree.  It was
considered and rejected on a measurement rather than on taste: react-redux
is the only package whose peers block React 19, so once the bindings are
required to be on a release that supports 19 there is nothing left for an
override to suppress.  A check for the mechanism instead of the property
would be a check of how, and this file grades what is true of the tree.
- Manual memoisation, the ninety-four sites of it.  That is the compiler
step's subject and removing it here would spend it early.
- The router major.  Also a later step's.
The guard used on everything carried forward is react at major 19 together
with bindings that support it.  It is the marker for 'this step has begun',
the same role concurrent-hooks-used played at step 5: a tree that has not
moved the runtime has not done this step, and the fifteen checks that ask
whether it broke anything must not pay it for standing still.  Both halves
are read off the installed tree, not off package.json, and the built-from-
source precondition is what ties the tree those readings come from to the
site the behavior family drove.
Measured before this file was written, all on the step-5 reference solution:
- untouched, under this spec: every check 0, reward 0.45.
- upgraded (react 19.3.0, react-dom 19.3.0, react-redux 9.3.0, propTypes
removed) under step 5's spec: 210/210 behavior, entry 133,024 gzipped
before the screen in one chunk, 62 chunks, strict run 17/17/17 with 0
messages and React's development text present, and every step-5 gate at
1.0 except the two that pin major 18.
- React 19 with react-redux 7.2.9 forced by an overrides entry: installs,
builds, and reproduces the recorded behavior.  That is the shortcut
bindings-support-19 exists to close.

guard.why: The tree still builds, serves and behaves like the application, so that what the gates measure is a migration of it rather than its absence.
guard.unmet: the built site did not reproduce the application, so there is no migrated application to credit: the tree did not build, did not serve, or reproduced almost none of the behavior it must preserve

guard.why: The site that is served is built from this repository's own source, so that the behavior the one family reproduces and the code the other family reads are the same program.
guard.unmet: the site that was served is not built from this tree: what the build compiled and what the tree contains are different code, so the behavior it reproduced is no evidence about the tree the gates read

checks.why: The React that is installed is version 19. This is the version this whole migration line is named for and the step it is reached at: every earlier step was a move towards a runtime that had not arrived yet, and this is where it does. The reading is of the installed tree rather than of the range in package.json, and a tree with more than one major of React installed fails it, because a second copy left behind is the case a declared range cannot show.

And the renderer moved with it. React and its DOM renderer are one release in two packages and a tree holding them apart is not on either version; the separate id is here because the two are separately declared and separately installable, and the failure of leaving one behind is worth reading off gates.json by name.

The store bindings are from a release that supports React 19. This is the step's own forcing function and the reason it is a migration rather than a version string: the tree arrives holding react-redux 7.2.9, whose peer range stops at React 18, so an install of React 19 beside it fails outright and a half-done upgrade does not build at all. Two majors separate 7 from the first release that declares React 19 - v8 rewrote the subscription onto useSyncExternalStore and v9 dropped React below 18 - and that is the distance this step actually travels in the dependency graph. It is a check of its own rather than a consequence of the install because the conflict can be suppressed: an overrides entry in package.json makes npm install 7.2.9 beside React 19 without complaint, the application still builds, and it was measured reproducing every one of the recorded scenarios. A tree that did that is running a package outside the support its own author declares, which is the opposite of having migrated to one that supports the runtime.

No component still hangs a propTypes object on itself. React 19 removed propTypes from function components: the declarations are not checked, not warned about and not read - they are inert text that tells a reader the props are validated when nothing validates them. The tree arrives with three of them, one on each of the carousel's three components. This is the one construct of the five React 19 items this step's line names that has a subject in this repository, and it is graded as the step's own work rather than as tidying. It is also the key the inherited family is credited against: a tree still carrying the declarations has not done the one thing this step asks of its source, and the five steps behind it are not paid out to a tree that has not started. Keyed here rather than on the manifest line because the manifest line is clerical and this is the work.

And nothing imports the package any more. Deleting the assignment while leaving the import behind leaves the package in the module graph and in the bytes the browser downloads, doing nothing; leaving the object the assignment referred to while deleting the import is worse, because the object's own body reads PropTypes.array at module scope and the module throws before it exports anything. The second one is not hypothetical - it is what a first attempt at this removal actually produced here - and the two counts together are what make the removal complete rather than partial.

And it is not a dependency any more. A package nothing imports but package.json still declares is installed on every machine that builds this tree and audited on every machine that scans it; the source having stopped referring to it is half of removing it. Scored rather than made the key to the checks the tree carried in: leaving the line behind is one clerical omission in a file the candidate is already editing, and a step that has removed the declarations and the imports has happened whether or not the line went with them.

What a visitor waits for before anything renders is still under 140 KB gzipped, measured the way the step before this one measured it: the built site is opened at an address that renders the application's own no-such-route screen, and every piece of javascript the page asked for between the navigation and that screen appearing is summed gzipped. This is the one number the upgrade actually threatens. The tree arrives at 111,325 bytes there; React 19's runtime is larger than React 18's, and the same tree on 19 with the bindings that support it was measured at 133,024 - just under 22 KB more, and under 7 KB of room left against a budget that does not move. The budget does not move because the step before this one is what earned it, and a runtime upgrade is not a licence to hand back what was earned. A wall rather than a slope. It was written as a slope for one round, full weight at 140 KB and nothing at 160 KB, and the slope could never pay: the guard beside it reads the same 140,000 out of the settled total, the settled total is the sum the reading before the screen is a part of, so a tree over the budget at the cut is over it settled and the guard has already scored the check zero before the slope is consulted. Grading an interval no tree can be scored in is a sentence about the spec rather than about any tree, and §4 asks for a number, not for a gradient.

checks.why: React's development build, running the application under StrictMode at seventeen addresses, reports nothing. The tree arrives with this already true under React 18, and the question this step asks is whether it is still true under a new major whose development checks are not the same checks. Measured on the upgraded tree: seventeen addresses, seventeen rendered, seventeen showing their own screen, fifteen of the application's endpoints reached, zero messages. So the answer here is that React 19 says nothing about this tree that React 18 did not - which is a finding rather than an assumption, and it is worth a gate precisely because the cheap way to make a new major quiet is to stop listening.
